notes.title: Innovation: what it is and its four forms
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Innovation = something new that **creates value and gets used**.
- Four forms: **product, process, business model, market**.
- Engineers make it possible; this course is about whether it's worth building.

---

## In one line
**Innovation** is the successful introduction of something new (an idea, product, process or business model) that creates value for someone. Being new isn't enough: it has to be used and matter.

## Structure to write
**Four forms of innovation** (slide 4):
1. **Product**: a new or improved offering
2. **Process**: a better way of doing existing work
3. **Business model**: a new way of creating and capturing value
4. **Market**: an existing offering reaching a new audience

**Why engineers need this course** (slide 3):
- See opportunity, not just specs: from "build what's requested" to "spot what's needed"
- Think in prototypes, not perfection: test small, cheap versions first
- Bridge technical and human value: link what you can build to what people will use and pay for

**Engineer's role:** makes innovation technically possible, but technical possibility doesn't guarantee value. The gap is "can build it" vs "should build it".

## Remember it by
**P-P-B-M**: Product, Process, Business model, Market.

*Slides 3–4*

notes.title: Innovation vs invention
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Invention** = creating something new. Test: *does it work?*
- **Innovation** = turning an idea into adopted value. Test: *does it get used?*
- Most inventions never become innovations.

---

## In one line
Every innovation may start with an invention, but an invention only becomes an innovation once people actually adopt it.

## Structure to write (comparison table, slide 6)
| Aspect | Invention | Innovation |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | A new device, method or idea | Applying an idea to create adopted value |
| Primary question | "Can this be made?" | "Will this be used, and by whom?" |
| Where it happens | Lab, workshop, research setting | Market, business, real-world deployment |
| Requires | Technical knowledge, creativity | Technical knowledge + market insight + execution |
| Risk of failure | Low (no market exposure yet) | High (must survive customers and competition) |

Extra points (slide 5): invention can sit unused for decades; innovation needs a **business model**, not just a mechanism.

## Examples (slide 7)
| | Invention | Innovation |
|---|---|---|
| Steam engine | 1600s–1700s, pumping water | Railways and factories → Industrial Revolution |
| Telephone | 1876, voice over wire | Decades of network build-out → mobile/smartphones |
| IC engine | 1800s | Ford's moving assembly line made cars affordable |

## Why it matters (slide 8)
Inventing → judge by "does it work reliably?" Innovating → "who needs it, will they adopt it?" Most real projects need both: switch from *make it work* to *make it matter*.

*Slides 5–8*

notes.title: Entrepreneurial mindset: six traits
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Mindset ≠ starting a company: it's **founder instincts in technical work**.
- Six traits: **curiosity, problem-first, resourcefulness, calibrated risk, user empathy, resilience**.
- Arc: **Notice → Prototype → Validate → Scale**.

---

## In one line
An entrepreneurial mindset means approaching engineering with curiosity about unmet needs, comfort with uncertainty and a bias toward testing ideas in the real world.

## Structure to write
**Traditional vs entrepreneurial engineering** (slide 9)
| Traditional | Entrepreneurial |
|---|---|
| Given a spec, build to it precisely | Questions whether the spec solves a real problem |
| Optimises for correctness and reliability | Optimises for validated value, then reliability |
| Success = technical performance | Success = adoption and impact |

**Six traits** (slide 10)
1. **Technical curiosity**: dig into why a system behaves as it does, not just fix symptoms
2. **Problem-first thinking**: start from a real need, then choose the technology
3. **Resourcefulness**: working prototypes with limited time, budget or tools
4. **Calibrated risk-taking**: small, cheap experiments to test risky assumptions early
5. **User empathy**: how real people will use (or misuse) what you build
6. **Resilience**: failed prototypes and pivots are data, not defeat

**From problem to impact** (slide 11)
1. **Notice**: spot a real, recurring problem
2. **Prototype**: smallest working version that tests the core idea
3. **Validate**: put it in front of real users
4. **Scale**: refine on evidence, grow what's proven

## Remember it by
Traits: **C-P-R-R-U-R** (Curiosity, Problem-first, Resourcefulness, Risk, User empathy, Resilience).

*Slides 9–12*

notes.title: Types of innovation: incremental, disruptive, frugal
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Incremental** = improve what exists (low risk).
- **Disruptive** = start with an overlooked segment, then displace the leaders.
- **Frugal** = do more with less by redesigning, not just cutting.

---

## Structure to write
| | Incremental | Disruptive | Frugal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Definition | Small, continuous improvements to an existing product, service or process | New product/service for an overlooked or underserved segment that improves and eventually displaces established competitors | Simpler, more affordable solutions, often for resource-constrained markets, by rethinking design |
| Key traits | Improves efficiency, quality or features; same business model and market; common in mature industries | Starts "worse" by traditional metrics but solves a different problem; creates a new market or value network; leaders dismiss it | Affordability and accessibility; strips to core function without losing essential value; reverse innovation; resourcefulness over big R&D |
| Risk | Lower risk, lower cost, faster | Higher risk, potentially transformative reward | Low cost by design |
| Examples | Yearly iPhone models; flip-top toothpaste cap; better fuel efficiency each model year; app updates (dark mode) | Netflix vs Blockbuster; Uber/Ola vs taxis; digital cameras vs Kodak film; low-cost airlines | Tata Nano; Jaipur Foot; M-Pesa (Kenya); Aakash tablet |

**Reverse innovation:** a frugal innovation from an emerging market later moves into developed markets (slide 7).

## Classifying (slide 9)
Justify the type in one sentence; many real innovations **blend types**. From the deck's sorting list: new bristle pattern → incremental; SaaS replacing boxed software → disruptive; solar lanterns for off-grid villages → frugal; budget phone stripped of extras → frugal; new snack flavour → incremental; rural telemedicine app → frugal and disruptive.

## Takeaway (slide 12)
No one-size-fits-all: the right type depends on **goal, resources and market**, and big breakthroughs often combine all three.

*Types of Innovation deck, slides 1–12*

notes.title: Design thinking: definition and the three Ps
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Human-centred approach: **needs first, problems as opportunities, test before committing**.
- Aim for **desirable + feasible + viable**.
- People → desirability, Process → feasibility, Purpose → viability.

---

## In one line
**Design thinking** is a human-centred approach to innovation that puts real people's needs first, reframes problems as opportunities and rapidly tests ideas before committing to them.

## Structure to write (slide 3)
| P | Lens | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **People** | Desirability | Understand users deeply through empathy and observation |
| **Process** | Feasibility | Iterate quickly: build, test, learn, refine |
| **Purpose** | Viability | Deliver value that is sustainable for the business |

The sweet spot every solution aims for: **desirable, feasible and viable**.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 1–3*

notes.title: Five stages of design thinking; diverge vs converge
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test**.
- It's a **loop**: Test feeds back into Define and Ideate.
- Diverge = go wide (Empathize, Ideate, Prototype); converge = go narrow (Define, Select, Test).

---

## Structure to write (slide 4)
1. **Empathize**: understand users' needs, emotions and context
2. **Define**: synthesise insights into a clear problem statement
3. **Ideate**: generate a wide range of possible solutions
4. **Prototype**: quick, low-cost representations of ideas
5. **Test**: try prototypes with users and gather feedback

**Non-linear:** insights from Test go back into Define and Ideate, so it's a cycle, not a straight line.

## Diverge, then converge (slide 5)
| Diverge: expand possibilities | Converge: make focused choices |
|---|---|
| Empathize: gather many perspectives | Define: one sharp problem statement |
| Ideate: lots of ideas | Select: cluster and prioritise ideas |
| Prototype: explore multiple concepts | Test: validate and decide what stays |
| Defer judgment, seek quantity and variety | Analyse, prioritise, commit |

## Remember it by
**"Every Developer Is Probably Tired"**: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 4–5*

notes.title: Problem identification and framing techniques
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Solve the **right** problem before solving it right.
- Rules: **root cause, user's problem, evidence, narrow**.
- Tools: **5 Whys, How Might We, Point-of-View, problem statement**.

---

## In one line
Most failed products are well-built answers to the wrong question, so frame the problem before solving it.

## Structure to write
**Four rules** (slide 6)
1. **Symptom vs root cause**: look past what's visible to what's causing it
2. **User's problem, not yours**: frame it from the user's perspective
3. **Evidence over assumption**: ground it in observation and data
4. **Narrow and specific**: a focused problem is a solvable one

**Why it matters:** ~35% of startups fail because there was no real market need; fixing a problem framed correctly up front is ~5× cheaper than after build; one sharp statement aligns the team.

**Four framing techniques** (slide 7)
| Technique | What it does | Deck example |
|---|---|---|
| **5 Whys** | Ask "why?" repeatedly to drill from symptom to root cause | Why is checkout slow? → … → the API retries 3× on timeout |
| **How Might We** | Turn a pain point into an open, optimistic question | "How might we make first-time setup feel effortless?" |
| **Point-of-View** | User + need + insight in one sentence | "A busy nurse needs fast handoffs because errors cost lives." |
| **Problem statement** | Concise, testable definition and scope | "Users abandon onboarding at step 3 due to unclear input rules." |

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 6–7*

notes.title: Problem–solution fit and validating it
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Fit = a **validated problem** meets a solution that **really resolves it** for a defined group.
- Comes **before product–market fit**.
- Validate: **segment → pain → map → signal → measure**.

---

## In one line
**Problem–solution fit** is the point where a validated problem meets a solution that genuinely resolves it for a defined group of users. It comes before product–market fit.

## Structure to write
**Three conditions** (slide 8)
1. **Real, urgent problem**: people already look for workarounds
2. **Clear target segment**: you know exactly whose problem it is
3. **Solution resolves it**: measurably better than the alternatives

**Five steps to validate** (slide 9)
1. **Define the segment**: the customers who feel the pain most
2. **Confirm the pain**: interview users; look for workarounds and willingness to pay
3. **Map the solution**: sketch how it removes the pain, end to end
4. **Test with a signal**: landing page, prototype or concierge MVP to measure real interest
5. **Measure and decide**: adoption, retention, satisfaction → pivot or persevere

**Signal to look for:** users are disappointed when they can't use your solution.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 8–9*

notes.title: Ideation: brainstorming, SCAMPER, mind mapping
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Brainstorming**: quantity, build on others, defer criticism.
- **SCAMPER**: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other use, Eliminate, Reverse.
- **Mind map**: central theme → branches → sub-branches.

---

## Brainstorming (slide 11)
**Seven ground rules:** defer judgment; encourage wild ideas; go for quantity; build on ideas ("yes, and…"); stay focused on the How-Might-We; one conversation at a time; be visual.

**Running a session:** 1 **Frame** (open with a clear HMW) → 2 **Diverge** (silent solo ideas, then share) → 3 **Cluster** (group into themes) → 4 **Vote** (dot-vote) → 5 **Refine** (develop top picks into concepts).

## SCAMPER (slide 12)
| Letter | Prompt | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| S | Substitute | Swap a component, material or person |
| C | Combine | Merge two ideas, steps or features |
| A | Adapt | Adjust an idea from another context |
| M | Modify | Magnify, minify or reshape an element |
| P | Put to other use | Apply it to a new purpose or market |
| E | Eliminate | Remove parts to simplify |
| R | Reverse | Flip the order, roles or direction |

## Mind mapping (slide 13)
Start with the **central theme** in the middle → **branch** main ideas outward → add **sub-branches** for detail → **one keyword** per branch → **colour and images** to aid recall → **link** related branches.

## The whole flow (slide 14)
Identify the problem → Empathize & Define → Ideate (brainstorm, SCAMPER, mind map) → validate fit, and loop back when testing sharpens the problem.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 10–15*

notes.content:

notes.title: Venture modelling and unit economics
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- A venture model = a **testable one-page picture** of how a startup creates, delivers and captures value.
- Find the **riskiest assumption** and test it cheaply. Don't forecast perfectly.
- Formulas: **contribution = price − variable cost**, **break-even = fixed cost ÷ contribution**, **LTV:CAC ≥ 3**.

---

## In one line
**Venture modelling** is building a simple, testable picture of how a startup will create, deliver and capture value, and listing the assumptions that must be true for it to work.

## Structure to write
| Part | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Value creation** | Who is the customer, what is their problem, why is our solution better than today's workaround? |
| **Value delivery** | Which channels, operations, partners and resources do we need? |
| **Value capture** | Pricing, revenue, costs, margin: do we earn more than we spend? |
| **Evidence loop** | Assumption → experiment → data → decision: **pivot, persevere or stop** |

**How to apply:** list assumptions → rank by risk → draw a one-page model (canvas + unit economics) → test the riskiest one cheaply → update with evidence.

**Worked example (slide 3)**
- Price ₹500 − variable cost ₹300 = **₹200 contribution** per order
- Fixed cost ₹2,00,000/month ÷ ₹200 = **1,000 orders/month to break even**

## Three cases
| Case | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Dropbox** (USA, 2007) | Demo video before the product existed; waitlist 5,000 → 75,000 overnight | Test **demand** first, almost free |
| **Zerodha** (India, 2010) | Flat ₹20 or 0.03% per order (whichever lower); grew without VC money | **Unit economics** decide the model |
| **Tata Nano** (2008–2019) | ₹1 lakh car; seen as "cheapest car"; wound down 2019 | Cost model right, **status assumption never tested** |

## Remember it by
**Create → Deliver → Capture → Test.**

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 2–4*

notes.title: Value proposition canvas
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Two halves: **customer profile** (jobs, pains, gains) and **value map** (products, pain relievers, gain creators).
- **Fit** = your relievers and creators match the customer's top pains and gains, **proven with evidence**.
- Start from the customer's job, not your feature list. (Osterwalder & Pigneur)

---

## In one line
The **value proposition canvas** matches what customers need (their jobs, pains and gains) with what you offer, so the two fit.

## Structure to write (draw it)
| Value map: what you offer | ↔ | Customer profile: what they need |
|---|---|---|
| **Products & services**: app, device, service | ↔ | **Jobs**: what the customer is trying to get done |
| **Pain relievers**: remove or reduce pains | ↔ | **Pains**: obstacles, risks, costs, frustrations |
| **Gain creators**: create benefits they want | ↔ | **Gains**: outcomes and benefits they want |

**How to apply:** fill the customer profile first from interviews → rank pains and gains → design the value map for the top ones → test fit with evidence.

## Three cases
| Case | Job / pains | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Meesho** | Earn from home; no capital, unsold stock, shipping | Share catalogue on WhatsApp, no inventory, Meesho ships, reseller keeps margin |
| **Practo** (2008) | Find the right doctor fast; unclear availability, unverified info | Search by speciality, **reviews** (trust = gain creator), instant booking |
| **Aravind Eye Care** (1976) | Restore sight; cost, distance, lost wages | **Tiered pricing** (free/subsidised/paid), eye camps; paying patients cross-subsidise |

## Remember it by
**J-P-G ↔ P-R-C**: Jobs, Pains, Gains ↔ Products, Relievers, Creators.

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 5–6*

notes.title: Business model canvas: the nine blocks
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- A **one-page map of 9 blocks** showing how a business creates, delivers and captures value (Osterwalder & Pigneur).
- Start with **Customer Segments + Value Proposition**, then fill the rest.
- Read it as a story: partners and activities **build** value, channels **deliver** it, revenue must **exceed cost**.

---

## Structure to write (draw the canvas)
| Key Partners | Key Activities | Value Propositions | Customer Relationships | Customer Segments |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Who are our partners/suppliers? | What must we do best? | What value, which problem? | How do we get, keep, grow customers? | Who are we creating value for? |
| | **Key Resources**: people, IP, tech, cash | | **Channels**: app, stores, partners | |

| Cost Structure | Revenue Streams |
|---|---|
| Biggest fixed and variable costs | What customers pay for, how, how much |

**How to apply:** segments + value proposition → other blocks → check revenue > cost → test each block with evidence.

## Three cases
| Case | Key blocks | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Zomato (now Eternal)** | Segments: diners + restaurants. Revenue: commissions, ads, fees, Gold. Costs: rider payouts, discounts | Marketplace: each revenue stream ties to a segment; keep **both sides** happy |
| **Amul** (1946) | Partners: village societies → district unions → GCMMF. Costs: procurement, cold chain | Farmers are **suppliers and owners** |
| **Freshworks** (Nasdaq 2021) | SMB segment, tiered subscriptions, free plan | Recurring revenue; **free plan = main channel** |

## Remember it by
Left side = **efficiency** (partners, activities, resources, cost). Right side = **value** (relationships, channels, segments, revenue). Centre = **value proposition**.

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 7–8*

notes.title: Customer segments, revenue streams and cost structure
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Segments** = who pays, **revenue streams** = how they pay, **cost structure** = what it costs to serve them.
- Start with a small **beachhead** segment in urgent pain.
- Viable only if revenue per customer − cost to serve and acquire stays **positive at scale**.

---

## Structure to write
| Customer segments | Revenue streams | Cost structure |
|---|---|---|
| **Mass market**: one broad need (Jio) | **Product sale** (Lenskart) | **Fixed**: salaries, rent, tech |
| **Niche**: a specific need | **Subscription** (Freshworks) | **Variable**: materials, delivery, payment fees |
| **Segmented**: groups with different needs | **Transaction fee** (Razorpay) | **CAC**: cost to acquire a customer |
| **Multi-sided**: linked groups (Zomato) | **Commission** (Zomato) | Cost-driven vs value-driven |
| | **Advertising** (Meesho sellers) | Scale lowers cost per unit |
| | Freemium, licensing, leasing | |

## Formulas
- **Contribution margin** = price − variable cost
- **Break-even units** = fixed cost ÷ contribution margin
- **Healthy LTV:CAC** ≈ 3 or more

## Three cases
| Case | Money model | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Reliance Jio** (2016) | Mass market; free launch, then cheap data (₹99 + ₹303/month); 100M users in 170 days | Huge fixed cost works only with **huge volume** |
| **Lenskart** (2010) | Product sale; designs and makes in-house, own stores and app | **Vertical integration** lowers variable cost |
| **Razorpay** (2014) | B2B; small % fee per payment + add-ons | Revenue grows with customers' success; margin hit by bank fees |

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 9–10*

notes.title: IP basics: six types and durations in India
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **IP** = legal ownership of creations of the mind, so others can't copy them.
- Six types: **patent, trademark, copyright, design, GI, trade secret**. Learn the table.
- **File before public disclosure**; use NDAs and IP-assignment agreements.

---

## Structure to write (the table)
| IP type | Protects | Duration in India |
|---|---|---|
| **Patent** | New, inventive, industrially useful inventions | **20 years** from filing |
| **Trademark** | Brand names, logos, slogans | **10 years**, renewable |
| **Copyright** | Original works: code, content, music | **Author's life + 60 years** |
| **Design** | Shape or look of a product | **10 years + 5** extension |
| **Geographical Indication** | Products tied to a region | **10 years**, renewable |
| **Trade secret** | Confidential formulas, know-how | No registration; **while secret** |

**How to apply:** identify what's valuable → pick the IP type → file before disclosure → NDAs + IP assignment with founders, staff, vendors.

**Startup India (DPIIT-recognised):** **80%** rebate on patent fees, **50%** on trademark fees, fast-track patent examination, free IP facilitators.

## Three cases
| Case | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Turmeric patent** | US patent (1995) on turmeric for wounds; CSIR showed Sanskrit texts as **prior art**; revoked 1997; India built **TKDL** | Patent needs novelty; search before filing |
| **Darjeeling Tea** | India's **first GI** (2004–05, GI Act 1999); Tea Board licenses the logo | GI protects a shared regional name |
| **Coca-Cola formula** | Never patented since 1886; kept as **trade secret**; brand = trademark | Patent = time-limited + disclosure; secret lasts only while secret |

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 11–12*

notes.title: Ethics in entrepreneurship
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Ethics = **honest, fair, responsible** decisions for all stakeholders, even when the law doesn't force you.
- Four pillars: **honesty, safety & quality, data privacy, governance & fairness**.
- Legal is the minimum. **Trust** is slow to build and fast to lose.

---

## Structure to write
| Pillar | Means |
|---|---|
| **Honesty** | No inflated metrics, false claims or hidden risks to investors or customers |
| **Safety & quality** | Don't ship harmful products; act and recall fast |
| **Data privacy** | Collect only what you need, with consent; **DPDP Act, 2023** |
| **Governance & fairness** | Accurate accounts, no conflicts of interest, fair to staff and vendors |

**Stakeholders:** customers, employees, investors, partners, society.

**How to apply:** code of conduct → **front-page test** for big decisions → accurate records → protect user data → safe way to raise concerns.

## Three cases
| Case | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Theranos** (USA) | Claimed finger-prick blood tests; inflated results shown; closed 2018; Holmes convicted 2022, 11+ years | Overclaiming is **fraud**; in health it costs lives |
| **Johnson & Johnson** (1982) | Tylenol laced with cyanide, 7 deaths; recalled ~31M bottles, tamper-proof packaging; trust recovered | **Customers before profit**, communicate openly |
| **Satyam** (India, 2009) | Raju admitted inflating profits/cash by ~₹7,000 crore; rescued by Tech Mahindra; convicted 2015 | False accounts and weak **governance** destroy value |

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 13–14*

notes.title: Sustainability for startups
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Triple bottom line**: profit, people, planet.
- Four levers: **reduce, include, reuse & recycle, measure & report** (no greenwashing).
- Strongest when it **lowers cost or opens a market**, not as decoration.

---

## In one line
Sustainability means building ventures that create economic value while reducing harm to (and ideally benefiting) people and the planet.

## Structure to write
| Lever | Means |
|---|---|
| **Reduce** | Less energy, water, material in making and delivering |
| **Include** | Fair pay, local sourcing, access for under-served people |
| **Reuse & recycle** | Circular models keep materials in use |
| **Measure & report** | Claims need data; avoid **greenwashing** |

**How to apply:** map impact along the value chain → pick 1–2 measurable targets → redesign materials, energy, waste → test whether customers pay or costs fall.

**SDG links:** 7 Clean energy, 8 Decent work, 9 Industry & innovation, 12 Responsible consumption, 13 Climate action.

## Three cases (three levels)
| Case | Level | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bakeys Foods** (Hyderabad, 2011) | Product | Edible spoons from sorghum, rice, wheat; decompose in days | In 2016 cost ~2× plastic: close the **price gap** |
| **Patagonia** (USA) | Business model | 1% of sales to causes; repair/resell; 2022 ownership to a trust | Sustainability can shape **ownership** |
| **Cochin Intl. Airport** (Kerala) | Infrastructure | World's **first fully solar airport** (2015); UN Champions of the Earth 2018 | One-time capital cost cut a recurring cost |

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 15–16*

notes.title: Startup pitching: types and audience questions
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- A pitch = a **short, structured, persuasive** presentation that helps a specific audience make a specific decision.
- Five types by length: **elevator, demo day, competition, investor, sales**.
- Not a product tour: an **argument backed by evidence, ending in a clear ask**.

---

## Structure to write
| Type | Length | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| **Elevator pitch** | 30–60 seconds | Earn a follow-up conversation |
| **Demo day pitch** | 2–3 minutes | Get investor meetings |
| **Competition / hackathon** | 5–7 minutes | Win the award and visibility |
| **Investor pitch** | 10–20 min + Q&A | Win funding |
| **Sales pitch** | Varies | Win a customer |

**How to apply:** know the audience and decision → story: **hook, problem, solution, proof, ask** → rehearse to time → answer honestly.

**Five questions every audience asks:** Why this problem? Why you? Why now? What's the proof? What do you need from us?

## Three cases
| Case | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **iPhone launch** (Jan 2007) | "Three revolutionary products" repeated until the audience saw one device; live demo | One idea + repetition + demo |
| **YC Demo Day** (W2015) | 114 startups, ~2.5 min each: problem, solution, growth, team | In short slots **clarity beats completeness** |
| **Shark Tank India S1** | ~62,000 applied, 198 pitched; ask implies valuation (₹50 lakh for 5% = ₹10 crore) | **Know your numbers**; credibility is won in Q&A |

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 17–18*

notes.title: Elements of an effective pitch deck
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- A pitch deck tells investors the story: **problem, solution, market, model, proof, team, ask**.
- **Ten slides**, each answering one investor question.
- Rules: 10–12 slides, one idea per slide, **Kawasaki 10/20/30**, numbers over adjectives.

---

## Structure to write (the 10 slides)
| # | Slide | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title & hook | What do you do, in one line? |
| 2 | Problem | Whose pain, and how big? |
| 3 | Solution | How do you fix it? |
| 4 | Product / demo | What does it look like? |
| 5 | Market size | How big can it get? |
| 6 | Business model | How do you make money? |
| 7 | Traction | What proof already exists? |
| 8 | Competition & moat | Why will you win? |
| 9 | Team | Why are you the ones? |
| 10 | Ask & use of funds | What do you need, for which milestones? |

**How to apply:** one-sentence story first → one headline per slide → one proof point per slide → cut what doesn't support the ask.

**Kawasaki 10/20/30:** 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point font.

## Three cases
| Deck | Facts | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Airbnb** (2009) | ~10 slides; "Book rooms with locals, rather than hotels"; 10% commission; raised ~$600K incl. Sequoia | **Simplicity**, one idea per slide |
| **UberCab** (2008) | 25 slides; US taxi market ~$4.2B; $200K pre-seed; story jumped around | Order slides to flow; include **why now** |
| **Buffer** (2011) | ~$500K seed; deck shared publicly; built on **transparent metrics** | Real traction beats big market claims |

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 19–20*

notes.title: Storytelling for startups
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Turn facts into a narrative: **character, problem, turning point, result**.
- Structure: **Hero → Struggle → Guide → Plan → Success**. The **customer** is the hero, not the founder.
- Data convinces the mind; story moves the decision: **one story + one number**.

---

## Structure to write
| Step | Is |
|---|---|
| **Hero** | A real customer |
| **Struggle** | The problem moment |
| **Guide** | Your venture |
| **Plan** | How the product helps |
| **Success** | Result and stakes |

**How to apply:** one customer as hero → vivid problem moment → solution as guide → prove the result with a number → clear ask.

| Do | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Concrete scenes, plain words | Jargon, feature lists |
| One human example + one number | Founder as the hero |
| Customer as hero | Stories with no stakes or result |

## Three cases
| Case | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Dollar Shave Club** (2012) | ~$4,500 funny video mocking overpriced razors; 12,000 orders in 48 h; Unilever bought it ~$1B (2016) | Tone + clear "villain" + simple offer |
| **Paper Boat** (2013) | "Drinks and Memories"; jaljeera, aamras; childhood nostalgia | Emotion can **create a category** |
| **Amul girl** (since 1966) | Witty topical hoardings + "Utterly Butterly Delicious" | A consistent character builds recognition for decades |

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 21–22*

notes.title: Elevator pitch and investor pitch
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Elevator pitch**: 30–60 s, earns a follow-up. **Investor pitch**: 10–15 min + Q&A, asks for a decision.
- Learn the **30-second formula** word for word.
- Valuation = ask ÷ equity %: ₹1 crore for 1% = ₹100 crore.

---

## The 30-second formula
> For **[customer]** who **[problem]**, **[Company]** is a **[category]** that **[key benefit]**. Unlike **[alternative]**, we **[difference]**. We have **[proof]**. We seek **[ask]**.

## Investor pitch flow
Hook (30 s) → Problem → Solution & demo → Market → Business model → Traction → Competition → Team → Financials & ask → **10+ min Q&A**

**Questions investors ask:** How will you get customers, at what cost? What are your margins? What if a big player copies you? What will you do with the money?

**Rehearse in 4 steps:** 1. Write it out (30 s and 5 min) → 2. Time it → 3. Record & review (jargon, filler, speed) → 4. Mock Q&A

## Three cases
| Case | What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Airbnb one-liner** | "Book rooms with locals, rather than hotels": action, product, difference | If a stranger can repeat it, it works |
| **Revamp Moto** (Shark Tank India S1) | Asked ₹1 cr for 1% (₹100 cr valuation); closed at ₹1 cr for 1.5% (~₹67 cr) with Aman Gupta & Anupam Mittal | Know valuation logic and minimum terms |
| **YC Rehearsal Day** | Dress rehearsal a week before Demo Day; Paul Graham: explain what you do and why users want it | Rehearse with critics; cut the rest |

## Remember it by
Clear in **30 seconds**, convincing in **5 minutes**, defensible under **questions**.

*EM Units 4–5 deck, slides 23–24*

notes.title: EM Unit 4 — one-page revision sheet
notes.content:
**No exam pattern announced yet.** Write answers as *definition → structure (table or canvas) → one case*.

| Topic | The structure to reproduce | Slides |
|---|---|---|
| Venture modelling | create / deliver / capture / evidence loop; break-even worked example | 3–4 |
| Value proposition canvas | jobs, pains, gains ↔ products, pain relievers, gain creators | 5–6 |
| Business model canvas | the 9 blocks drawn as the canvas | 7–8 |
| Segments, revenue, cost | 4 segment types, 6 revenue types, fixed/variable/CAC; 3 formulas | 9–10 |
| IP | 6-row table: type, protects, duration | 11–12 |
| Ethics | 4 pillars + front-page test | 13–14 |
| Sustainability | triple bottom line + 4 levers + SDGs | 15–16 |

**One-liners**
- Contribution = price − variable cost · break-even = fixed ÷ contribution · LTV:CAC ≥ 3.
- Patent 20 · trademark 10 (renewable) · copyright life + 60 · design 10 + 5 · GI 10 (renewable) · trade secret while secret.
- Dropbox tested demand, Zerodha designed unit economics, Nano never tested status.
- Theranos lied, J&J protected customers, Satyam falsified accounts.

notes.title: EM Unit 5 — one-page revision sheet
notes.content:
**No exam pattern announced yet.** Write answers as *definition → structure → one case*.

| Topic | The structure to reproduce | Slides |
|---|---|---|
| Pitching | 5 pitch types × length × goal; 5 audience questions | 17–18 |
| Pitch deck | the 10 slides + the question each answers; Kawasaki 10/20/30 | 19–20 |
| Storytelling | Hero → Struggle → Guide → Plan → Success; do / avoid | 21–22 |
| Elevator & investor | 30-second formula; investor flow; 4 rehearsal steps | 23–24 |

**One-liners**
- A pitch is an argument backed by evidence, ending in a clear ask, not a product tour.
- Elevator 30–60 s · demo day 2–3 min · competition 5–7 min · investor 10–20 min + Q&A.
- Valuation = ask ÷ equity: ₹50 lakh for 5% = ₹10 crore.
- Airbnb = simplicity, Uber = loose narrative, Buffer = real numbers.
- Dollar Shave Club = a video, Paper Boat = a feeling, Amul = a character.
